Hay Fever and Riding: Managing Allergies on Tour

Hay fever affects approximately 20% of the UK population, and riding a motorcycle through pollen-rich countryside can make symptoms significantly worse. Sneezing inside a helmet at 60mph is unpleasant and potentially dangerous. Here's how to manage allergies and keep riding.

The Pollen Calendar

  • March-April: Tree pollen (birch, oak, plane). Worst in woodland areas and towns with avenue trees.
  • May-July: Grass pollen — the most common trigger. Peak season. Rural areas and farmland are worst.
  • July-September: Weed pollen (nettle, dock). Generally milder than grass pollen.

Medication Strategies

  • Non-drowsy antihistamines: Cetirizine, loratadine, or fexofenadine. Take them daily during your pollen season, not just when symptoms appear. Start two weeks before your expected exposure.
  • Nasal spray: Steroid nasal sprays (Beconase, Pirinase) reduce inflammation and are very effective. Use daily.
  • Eye drops: Sodium cromoglicate drops prevent itchy eyes. Apply before riding.
  • Timing: Take medication in the evening — most antihistamines work for 24 hours and taking them at night means any drowsiness occurs during sleep.

Riding Adjustments

  • Visor down: Keep your visor fully closed to reduce pollen reaching your nose and eyes. A Pinlock or anti-fog insert prevents fogging.
  • Buff or balaclava: A fabric covering over your nose and mouth acts as a basic pollen filter.
  • Regular visor cleaning: Pollen sticks to visors and reduces visibility. Clean with visor cleaner at every stop.
  • Avoid peak pollen times: Pollen counts are highest in late morning and early evening. Ride early morning or mid-afternoon when counts are lower.

Route Choices

  • Coastal routes: Sea breezes blow pollen inland, making coastal roads lower-pollen environments.
  • Mountain and moorland: Higher altitude means less grass pollen. Mountain passes are often lower-pollen than valley roads.
  • After rain: Rain washes pollen from the air. The hours after a rain shower are often the best riding for hay fever sufferers.
Don't let hay fever stop you touring. With proper medication (started before the season), sensible gear choices, and smart route planning, hay fever riders can enjoy the season almost as much as anyone else. A sneezy day on a motorcycle is still better than a sneezy day at a desk.

Long-Term Management

If hay fever significantly impacts your riding, consult your GP about immunotherapy treatments. These involve gradual exposure to allergens and can dramatically reduce symptoms over 2-3 years. For serious allergy sufferers, it's a long-term investment in better riding seasons.

Monitoring pollen forecasts helps you plan rides around low-count days. The Met Office provides daily pollen forecasts by region, and several apps offer hour-by-hour predictions. Cross-referencing pollen forecasts with weather forecasts helps you choose the best riding days.
keyTakeaways: Around 20% of the UK population has hay fever, and sneezing inside a helmet at 60mph is both unpleasant and dangerous.
Grass pollen (May-July) is the most common trigger and peaks in rural and farmland areas.
Start non-drowsy antihistamines around two weeks before your season and take them daily, not just when symptoms appear.
Keep the visor fully closed with an anti-fog insert, and a buff or balaclava acts as a basic pollen filter.
Coastal, mountain, and post-rain routes carry lower pollen loads than inland valleys and grassland.

faq.q: When should I start taking hay fever medication?
faq.a: Start non-drowsy antihistamines such as cetirizine, loratadine, or fexofenadine around two weeks before your expected exposure, and take them daily through the season rather than only when symptoms flare. Steroid nasal sprays and sodium cromoglicate eye drops used daily add further protection. Taking antihistamines in the evening means any drowsiness happens during sleep.

faq.q: How can I reduce pollen while riding?
faq.a: Keep your visor fully closed with a Pinlock or anti-fog insert to stop pollen reaching your nose and eyes. A buff or balaclava over the nose and mouth acts as a basic filter. Clean your visor at every stop, since pollen sticks to it and reduces visibility, and ride early morning or mid-afternoon when counts are lower than late morning and early evening.

faq.q: Which routes are best for pollen-sensitive riders?
faq.a: Coastal roads benefit from sea breezes that blow pollen inland, and higher-altitude mountain and moorland routes carry much less grass pollen than valley roads. The hours after a rain shower are often the best riding of all, as rain washes pollen from the air.

faq.q: Is there a long-term fix for hay fever?
faq.a: If hay fever seriously affects your riding, ask your GP about immunotherapy. This involves gradual, controlled exposure to allergens and can dramatically reduce symptoms over two to three years. For severe sufferers it is a worthwhile long-term investment in better riding seasons.
